opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when we started the s1 project, we initially used Gemini's Flash Thinking model to generate the reasoning traces, because at the time it was one of the few models that actually exposed its thinking. But once DeepSeek R1 came out, we switched over and found it worked noticeably better for our purposes.

There are a few reasons for that. First, R1 is just a stronger reasoner on the kinds of hard math and science questions we were curating, so the traces are more likely to end in a correct answer, and the reasoning along the way tends to be higher quality. When you're only fine-tuning on a thousand examples, the quality of each individual trace matters enormously. You can't afford noisy or wrong reasoning in there.

Second, R1's traces are long and really exhibit the behaviors you want the student model to pick up: it double-checks itself, it backtracks, it says things like "wait, let me reconsider," it explores alternative approaches. Those are exactly the patterns that seem to matter for test-time scaling, and distilling from R1 transfers them quite effectively.

And third, there's an openness aspect. R1 is an open-weights model with a permissive license, so the full reasoning is available to you and you're on firmer ground using its outputs for training. That fits with our goal of making everything in s1 fully open: the data, the model, the code, so others can reproduce and build on it.

So in our ablations, swapping the Gemini traces for R1 traces gave us a meaningful bump on benchmarks like AIME and MATH, which is why we released the updated s1.1 model trained on the R1 data.

r001.rationale: The response says R1 is open weights and that its full reasoning is available, identifying accessible thinking traces as an advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when we built s1, the whole point was to take a really small set of questions, around a thousand, and pair them with high-quality reasoning traces, then fine-tune a Qwen model on them. So the quality of those traces matters a lot, because that's basically all the model is learning from.

Our first version used Gemini's thinking traces. And those worked, but Gemini only gave us a kind of summarized version of its reasoning. It wasn't the raw chain of thought. It was cleaner, shorter, a bit sanitized. And when you distill from that, you're teaching the model a compressed style of thinking rather than the actual process.

When R1 came out, two things changed. First, the model is open, so we get the full, unfiltered reasoning trace. All the backtracking, the "wait, let me reconsider," the self-verification steps. That's the behavior we actually want the student model to pick up, because that's what seems to drive the gains from test-time compute. If you train on the messy version, the model learns to be messy in a productive way, and then budget forcing, where we append "wait" and let it keep going, works much better because the model has actually seen what it looks like to continue reasoning.

Second, R1 was just stronger on the hard math and competition-style problems we cared about. So the traces are more often correct, and more often correct for the right reasons. With s1.1, we swapped in R1 traces on the same thousand questions and saw a solid jump on AIME and MATH, with nothing else changing. That's a pretty clean signal that the trace source was the bottleneck.

And then there's a practical point. Having an open model means reproducibility. Anyone can regenerate the data, inspect it, filter it differently. With a closed API, you're somewhat at the mercy of whatever the provider decides to expose, and that can change under you.

r001.rationale: The response says R1 is open and provides access to full, unfiltered reasoning traces, unlike Gemini’s summarized traces.

astra-6.text: I think the main advantage is that R1 gives you access to the full thinking trace. If you want to train a model to reason, you need more than just the final answer—you want the intermediate reasoning that led to it. With models that keep that reasoning hidden, you can’t directly use it as training data. R1 makes that possible, so it’s a useful option for generating traces that you can then distill into a smaller model.

r001.rationale: It says R1 provides access to the full thinking trace, making those intermediate reasoning steps usable as training data.

sol-6.1.text: I think the main advantage is that R1 makes its reasoning traces available. If you want to train a model to reason, you can use those traces as examples of how to work through a problem, rather than just training on the final answer. With a model that hides its reasoning, you don’t have that same access. So R1 is a much more practical option for generating that kind of training data.

r001.rationale: The response says R1 makes its reasoning traces available and that they can be used as examples to train reasoning, making it a more practical source of training data.
